5080.heavy: Heavy = [CVC], [CV˘] (long vowel) or [CVV9] (vowel + non-syllabic vowel / diphthong); light = [CV(] (short open syllable). (p. 21)
5080.dflt: Not applicable as stated: every lexeme contains exactly one heavy syllable, in final position (monosyllable = H, disyllable = LH); sequences *LL are excluded and HH sequences are two lexemes (pp. 21-22).
5080.prule: Family-level (pan-Chapakura) rule that the author applies to all eleven Chapakura languages including Yaru: stress is non-contrastive and predictable from syllable weight; the heavy syllable (CVC, CV: or CVV) is stressed and high-pitched, the light syllable (short open CV) unstressed and low-pitched. Because every lexeme is either a heavy monosyllable or a light+heavy disyllable, the stressed syllable is always the lexeme-final one: # (σ) σ # / → [ (σ̀) ˈσ́] (formula checked on p. 23). In casual registers, where up to three lexemes fuse into one phonological word, stress still sits on the heavy syllables (Moré [ˈkxaː ˈʔɔn] → [ˈkxɔn], p. 22), which is why the source's own weight framing, not a surface 'final' reading, is coded.
5080.srule: Not mentioned in Angenot 2013 [1997] (§2.1-2.2 pp. 21-23, §3.10 Yaru pp. 56-57, §4.2.2 p. 68, ch. 5 pp. 144-149 read): the source assigns one stress per lexeme and lexemes are at most disyllabic (light + stressed heavy), with no secondary or rhythmic stress discussed.

5081.tone: Tone language: two level tones (H, L) and two contour tones (rising, falling) per Bôt 2011a p. 89; four tonemes with lexical minimal pairs per Bouh 2004 pp. 38–39 (Tableau 3 p. 39). tn.translation: Yasa is a Bantu language of the equatorial coast spoken in Cameroon and Equatorial Guinea by ten thousand speakers. It is a noun-class language and a tone language: two level tones (high and low) and two contour tones (falling and rising), whose basic syllable structure is of the type (consonant) + vowel, (C)V.
tn.cite: Bôt, Dieudonné Martin Luther. 2011. Les verbes dérivés du yasa. Journal of West African Languages XXXVIII.1: 89–98 (Université de Douala).
tn.note: Four tones: high, low, falling, rising; minimal pairs in Bouh 2004: 38 (mbókà 'village' vs mbòkà 'prisoner'). A floating low from an elided prefix vowel docks as rising or long low. 5082.dflt: first syllable of the word (disyllables with open second syllable, trisyllabic monomorphemes, inflected final verbs and Medial verbs without Different Subject marking); penultimate in a listed set of trisyllables; unpredictable in 4-5 syllable monomorphemes
5082.prule: One primary stress per phonological word; stress non-contrastive. Default first-syllable stress (disyllables with open second syllable 'almost always'; trisyllabic monomorphemes 'usually'; inflected final verbs 'usually'). Heavy syllables attract stress: closed syllables, long vowels and diphthongs, and weakly the vowel /u/ — in (C)V.CVC disyllables 'most' have final stress (with 'quite a few exceptions', Table 2.8); long vowels 'usually stressed' (p. 2); diphthongs created by verbal suffixation take the stress (ongo-i [ɔˈŋɔɪ], iso-un-a [iˈsɔu.na]); monosyllabic V-final verb root + /u/-nucleus suffix (-nung, -gu-ng) stressed finally. Four- and five-syllable monomorphemes: 'stress is unpredictable'. Verbs and non-verbs follow different systems; stress in verbs is 'predictable', in nouns 'not entirely predictable' (p. 66).
5082.srule: Secondary stress is placed by verbal morphology: Near Future inflections carry a secondary stress on -ka-, the first element of the historical auxiliary (dawi-wang-ka-t [ˈda.βi.waŋˌkhat˺]); in past Habitual Dependent verb=it- 'be' fusions the inflected auxiliary bears only secondary stress, with primary stress on the first syllable of the lexical root ([ˈɔng.ɔng.itːˌduŋ]); the Completive enclitic =dup bears secondary stress. No general or rhythmic secondary-stress rule is stated for other words; secondary marks otherwise appear only in transcriptions (Hesienare [ˌhɛ.si.jɛˈna.rɛ], nimbuharak-ni [ˌni.mbu.haˈrak.ni], humbor-un-a [ˈhu.mbɔˌru.na]).

Pitch or F0 is not an acoustic correlate of stress in zsby, since this is a tonal language and F0 is used mainly to make tonal distinctions.

5085.prule: Stress ('acento de intensidad') is phonemic and contrastive: the language is not tonal, vowel length and pitch only accompany stress without phonemic autonomy; the single word stress falls almost always on the first or the second syllable of the word regardless of the word's total syllable count, and its position is lexical, as minimal pairs with initial vs. second-syllable stress show (wíjla 'peinar' vs. wijlá 'flecha de cerbatana'; kájate 'cazabe' vs. kajáte 'frío'; jlíjani 'hijo' vs. jlijáni 'garrapata pequeña'). A small listed set of words carries third-syllable stress (wakuláya, walipópo...; terekáyu, morokóto are called unassimilated loans). Morphology interacts: adding the possessive suffix -ne (or any other possessive suffix) shifts the word stress one syllable to the left, unless it is already on the first syllable, in which case it stays (síja 'piedra' > síjane; mayúlu 'cuenta de collar' > máyulune; yáju 'espejo' > yájune).

5086.heavy: Primary stress: none; the source says stress goes to the first syllable 'regardless of the number of syllables or moras that make up the word'. Secondary stress only (p. 98): 'Mora counting in this language is based on the number of sonorant (including vocalic) segments in words. Non-syllabic sonorants (nasals, liquids and approximants) that occur in a preconsonantal environment (i.e. as an off-set C2 segment of a medial C1VC2 syllable) are counted as constituting one mora. Word-final sonorants are not considered as constituting a mora.' Obstruent codas and vowel length add no mora.
5086.dflt: not applicable (primary stress is initial regardless of syllable weight, in over 98% of words; the mora count only positions secondary stress)
5086.prule: Primary stress on the first syllable of the word, regardless of the number of syllables or moras (quantity-insensitive, count-blind): 1704 of 1730 nominals (over 98%) in Hosokawa's dictionary count, and always word-initial (on the first-order prefix) in conjugated verbs.
5086.srule: One secondary stress per word, placed by mora count from the word start (mora = each vowel plus each preconsonantal sonorant coda of a medial syllable; word-final sonorants, obstruent codas and vowel length add none): on the 3rd mora if it is a vowel, otherwise on the 4th-mora vowel unless that vowel is word-final, in which case none (Table 314: cv'.cv.cv` dyanadya, cv'.s.cv` dyimbu, cv'.cv.cv`.cv wanangarri, but cv'.cv.s.cv kardimba with no secondary). In polymorphemic words morphology overrides the count: first syllable of the (first) suffix, of the non-initial compound member and of the reduplicant, and the root-initial syllable in conjugated verbs.

5088.dq: The domain of primary stress is the phonological word. All clitics are lexically stressed and do not affect the assignment of primary stress
5088.dloc: p. 111 (introduction: two degrees of stress, heavy = final consonant or long vowel, primary = rightmost stress); p. 112 sec. 1 (domain), sec. 1.1 Verbal Stress, sec. 1.2 Nominal Stress; p. 113 coronal-obstruent codas light, examples (4)-(6); p. 114 rules (7)-(8) and exceptions (9); p. 115 exceptions (10)-(11) and sec. 1.3 Exceptions to verb stress assignment; pp. 127-128 generalisation (65).
5088.heavy: Heavy syllables are defined as having either a final consonant or a long vowel nucleus (p. 111); for noun primary stress a word-final syllable closed by a coronal obstruent [-son, +cor] is considered light and not stressed, a final syllable closed by any other segment is heavy and stressed, and a final syllable with a long vowel is heavy even if closed by a coronal obstruent (p. 113); a word-final syllable ending in /n/ is always stressed (p. 127).
5088.dflt: penult (nouns with a light final syllable, e.g. [stápu] 'beans', [múkskut] 'fever'); verbs: ultima regardless of weight (or penult when a word-final inflectional suffix is extrametrical)
5088.prule: Nouns: primary stress on the final syllable if it is heavy (long vowel, or closed by any consonant other than a coronal obstruent), otherwise on the penult; word-final CV and CVC-with-coronal-obstruent-coda syllables are light/extrametrical. Secondary stress on every heavy syllable (CVC or CVV); primary stress = the rightmost stress in the phonological word. MacKay's formulation (7)-(8), p. 114: final light syllables extrametrical; build right-dominant quantity-sensitive feet; right-dominant word tree.
5088.srule: Secondary stress on every heavy syllable (closed syllable or long vowel: CVC, CVV); primary stress is the right-most of these stresses; a light CV syllable never bears secondary stress; predictable, so unmarked in MacKay's transcriptions. (MacKay 1994 sec. 6, per archive.org excerpt, additionally puts secondary stress on 'the first syllable of a word'; MacKay 1999 p. 73 and MacKay & Trechsel 2005 again say heavy syllables only.)

5094.dq: On two-syllable words with the same tone on both syllables the first syllable, i.e. the root, is pronounced with more power. If an ensuing syllable, i.e. the stem vowel or a suffix, carries a higher tone than the root, this gives the impression of stress, and indeed, such a syllable is pronounced with more power than a stem vowel syllable with a lower tone.
5094.prule: No stress rule stated as such: Yemsa is a three-level tone language (L, M, H, plus a rising tone). The author declines to describe stress in detail and offers a hedged observation: in disyllabic words with level tone the first syllable (the root) is pronounced with more force; a following stem vowel or suffix with a higher tone than the root is perceived as stressed, which she says may be just an effect of the high tone. Phonetic correlate: CV monosyllables lengthen their vowel under stress.

5099.tone: Kongo is tonal. Laman 1936 §22: the monosyllabic radicals show 'quatre tons très caractéristiques' (bas/grave, haut fort accentué, haut, moyen), 'Ces quatre tons des radicaux servent à former les quatre principales classes tonales, qui sont l’origine des tons sémantiques et des tons grammaticaux. Ils constituent aussi le principe de la notation mélodique dans le dictionnaire'. §19 ties tone to intensity and length (high, long, rising/falling syllables are more intense; 'L’ultième au ton plus haut que la syllabe précédente a toujours une très grande intensité') and separates this 'intensité mélodique' from 'l’accent d’intensité ou même, tout simplement, l’accent'; §20 says tone may weaken but never remove the root accent. Laman & Heinitz 1922 §28: 'The strong stress in the Kongo language may be placed on different syllables, whether they are high or low, rising or falling, because pitch and position in the sentence may have a strong influence upon the accent' (scan 'maj', 'risini', '£' normalised). De Clercq 1907 p. 451 marks long vowels with a macron and 'l’accent tonique par ’' and says speakers draw out long vowels 'en haussant légèrement la voix d’une façon presque chantante', but states no tone system and no placement rule.

5100.dq: In Mary's River, it falls on the first syllable of a stem; in Tualatin and Yoncalla, stress is often shifted to prefixed elements. If a prefix is added in Mary's River, stress does not move: wau·tso?, kuwau·tso?. [...] Falling pitch is a good deal more frequently marked than is rising pitch. 5100.dloc: Thesis: p.45, section 'Suprasegmentals'; summary sentence p.49 (p.57; 'Phonemic stress occurs on the first syllable of stems, and is accompanied by higher (or perhaps sometimes by lower) pitch'); printed = pdf - 8. 5100.heavy: Not applicable. The source states that stress 'occurs on both short and long vowels, and is thus independent of length' (Mary's River data; Frachtenberg's transcriptions); ICSNL p.10: 'Stress is independent of length.'
5100.prule: No positional rule is stated for Yoncalla. The source's own object is Mary's River (Central Kalapuya), where phonemic stress, realized with higher pitch ('pitch accent'), falls on the first syllable of the stem and does not move under prefixation; Jacobs's family-general statement (unpublished ms, 'n.p.') puts pitch accent on every syllable felt to be an independent root. For Yoncalla the only content, in both Hajda 1976 loci, is the comparative clause that stress 'is often shifted to prefixed elements', i.e. it is not fixed on the stem-initial syllable and frequently lands on a prefix; where on the prefix string, and under what conditions, is not said. 5104.prule: Lexical pitch accent (mora-based 'ascending kernel' 昇り核 system), not stress: for an n-mora noun there are n+1 contrastive patterns, unaccented (mid pitch, marked !) or the pitch rise on any one of the n moras (kernel /「/ before that mora); the kernel position is a lexical property of the word and is not computable from mora count, syllable count or weight (e.g. 2-mora: !パナ 'nose' unaccented, 「プニ 'boat' initial, パ「ナ 'flower' final; 3-mora: !タタミ, 「ウイビ, ワ「ラビ, アブ「ラ). Restriction: a moraic phoneme (long-vowel second half, N, diphthong offglide) bears the kernel only in absolute word-final position.

5104.tone: The source treats the system entirely as pitch accent (アクセント, 核, ピッチの上昇位置): an 'ascending kernel' marks the mora where pitch rises; n-mora nouns show n+1 patterns including an unaccented type spoken at mid pitch; pitch range is small and 'delayed rise' is common (§3.3). The words 強勢/ストレス/強弱 (stress) do not occur anywhere in the article (a full-text search of the full text: 0 hits); intensity is mentioned only in passing: the initial-kernel type begins slightly higher and 'is pronounced strongly and clearly' while the unaccented type passes if said 'with a little less force, lower' (§3.3), and particle-focused pronunciation makes ヌ 'clearly high and strong' (§3.6, body text). Uwano refutes the earlier N-pattern (2-3 pattern) analyses of Hirayama et al. 1966, Sakimura 1986 and Nakamoto & Shinozaki 1989.

tn.translation: Yoron Higashi-ku dialect is not an N-pattern accent such as the 3-pattern type of earlier studies, but a 'Pn = n+1 multi-pattern accent system' distinguished by an 'ascending kernel'. ... From (8), n-mora words have n+1 distinctions, the types being distinguished from one another by the position of the pitch rise; i.e. a dialect with an ascending kernel /「/, and (8) is interpreted as (9). ... Kernel-less may be left unmarked, but when it must be shown '!' is prefixed, since it is pronounced at roughly 'mid' height. ... The accent of this dialect should be described by mora, not by syllable.

5106.prule: Youle Jino is a tone language (five tonemes 55, 44, 33, 35, 42 on the syllable; complex phonological and grammatical tone alternations, esp. in verb complexes). Stress is stated to be phonologically marginal ('does not carry much phonological significance'): only for disyllabic words is a weak-strong (iambic) stress pattern 'considered to exist', i.e. prominence on the second (final) syllable, realized as the tone pattern 33-55 with a slightly shorter first syllable; for monosyllables and for phonological domains exceeding three syllables the author posits no stress pattern at all (3-syllable domains are not addressed). No weight sensitivity, no contrastive stress, no exhaustive word-stress rule: coded as a tone language whose only stress statement is a partial, hedged, phonetic iambic pattern in disyllables.
5106.srule: Not mentioned in Hayashi 2009 (grammar), §1.3.2.1 ストレス p.32 (and §1.3.2.2 pp.32-33): the only stress statement is a weak-strong pattern in disyllables; no secondary or rhythmic stress is described.

tn.quote: 1.3.1 /T(声調) チノ語には55, 44, 33, 35, 42の5種の声調素が認められる。音節単位で見られる声調素において注意すべき点を以下に掲げる。55調(高平調, H) [55] 高く平らに発声する。44調(中平調, M) [44] 2音節語の後部要素に出現することが多い。33調(低平調, L) [22～33] 低く平らに発声する。2音節語の前部要素に現れることが多い。35調(上昇調, R) [35～24] 文法機能を表す語、あるいは借用語に多い。42調(下降調, F) [42～53] 高いところから落ちる。... 1.3.2.1 ストレス ストレスは音韻的に大きな意味を持っているわけではない。特に2音節語において、弱強型(iambic)のストレスパターンが存在していると考えられる。
tn.translation: 1.3.1 /T (tone). Five tonemes are recognised in Jino: 55, 44, 33, 35, 42. Points to note about the tonemes, observed per syllable, are listed below. Tone 55 (high level, H) [55]: pronounced high and level. Tone 44 (mid level, M) [44]: often occurs on the second element of disyllabic words. Tone 33 (low level, L) [22~33]: pronounced low and level; often appears on the first element of disyllabic words. Tone 35 (rising, R) [35~24]: frequent in words expressing grammatical functions or in loanwords. Tone 42 (falling, F) [42~53]: falls from a high point. ... 1.3.2.1 Stress. Stress does not carry much phonological significance. …
